content:
Cytochalasin B is known to inhibit actin polymerization by binding to the plus end of actin filaments, which are microfilaments. Since microspikes of the growth cone contain actin-based microfilaments (not microtubules), exposure to cytochalasin B would cause depolymerization of these microfilaments.  
This effect is reversible upon removal of the drug, so the correct choice is reversible depolymerization of microfilaments in the microspike.  

Final answer: (C)
